metaDescription: Six key finder fobs compared on weight, thickness, beep volume and phone needs, from slim radio receivers to Bluetooth tags that ride on your key ring.
introParagraphs: A key finder fob is the small tag that lives on your key ring and either beeps when you call it or reports where it was last seen. The fob is the part you carry every day, so its size, weight and durability matter as much as its signal. A fob that snags pockets or dies quietly is worse than none.

We evaluated six fobs based on product specs and buyer feedback: the Jegoteer, JTD, Esky and Reyke radio receivers, plus the NVQ and Life360 Tile Bluetooth tags. We compared stated size, weight, beep volume, range, water rating and phone requirements, and we flagged where a listing gives no figures.
Use the tables below to match a fob to your key ring and your daily routine, then think about whether a phone belongs in the picture at all.

products.name: Jegoteer Lost Remote Finder, 4 Receivers, 131 ft
products.description:
The Jegoteer is a radio kit whose four oval receivers are the lightest fobs in this group, at about 5 g (0.17 oz) each. They measure roughly 1.9 x 1.2 x 0.3 inches and beep and flash when you press a button on the remote. The listing states an 85 dB beeper, a 131 ft range and a built-in LED flashlight.

It is described as a proven model for the past decade, with no app involved. Replacing the receiver button cell is done with a coin, and the transmitter takes two AAA batteries. The tradeoff is that the fobs are thicker than the 0.2 inch Esky receivers, and keys left outside the house cannot be found.

Because the fobs weigh so little, they suit a crowded key ring better than a bulky tag does. Keep the transmitter on a hook by the door. At 131 ft it matches the Reyke and JTD for reach, and at 85 dB it is louder than the Reyke's 80 dB or more.
products.bestFor: Anyone who wants a very light fob with a loud beep and a long radio reach.
pros: Each receiver weighs about 5 g, barely noticeable on a key ring
Stated 85 dB beeper is loud enough for cushions and drawers
Radio range stated at 131 ft through walls
Receiver cell can be changed with an ordinary coin
cons: Receivers are 0.3 inches thick, thicker than the slim Esky tags
Transmitter needs two AAA batteries on top of the fob cells
No map, so keys left away from home stay lost

products.name: JTD Key Finder Locator with Car Keychain Tracker
products.description:
The JTD kit includes two receivers and a car tracker keychain, aimed at people who mostly want to find car keys and a TV remote. The listing states an 85 dB beep and a range of 131 ft through walls. Attach a receiver to the key ring, press the button and follow the sound.

It is a small kit compared with four and six receiver sets, which keeps things simple for someone who only needs a couple of fobs. The listing also pitches the system as an all-in-one alternative to separate trackers. The tradeoff is the smaller count, and the listing does not give weight or thickness for the fobs.

If your problem is a single set of car keys and one remote, two fobs is enough, and you avoid buying extras that sit in a drawer. The remote still needs a hook. Against the Jegoteer's four fobs at 131 ft and 85 dB the JTD matches on specs but offers half the receivers, and unlike the Esky it does not state a thin profile.
products.bestFor: People who mainly want to find car keys and one TV remote.
pros: Includes a car keychain unit alongside two receivers
Stated 85 dB beep and flash through walls up to 131 ft
Small two-receiver set avoids paying for fobs you will not use
No phone, app or account needed to use it
cons: Only two receivers, fewer than the Jegoteer's four
Listing gives no weight or thickness for the fobs
Radio only, so keys left at a shop are not findable

products.name: Esky Key Finder Locator, 85 dB, 6 Receivers

specList.label: Battery
specList.value: CR2032 per receiver, up to 1 year

products.description:
The Esky has six receivers that are only about 0.2 inches thick, the slimmest fobs in this lineup. Each one flashes an LED and beeps at up to 85 dB when its button is pressed on the remote. The range is stated at 100 ft through walls, doors and furniture.

Thin fobs ride flatter on a key ring and snag less in a pocket, which is the main reason to choose this kit. Six fobs let you tag keys, a wallet, glasses and a spare set. The tradeoff is that range is shorter than the 131 ft kits, and each fob uses a CR2032 cell that needs replacing about once a year.

There is no phone or app involved, so it suits anyone who wants a plain beeper. Because there are six cells, set a single yearly date to swap them. The Esky fobs are thinner than the Jegoteer's 0.3 inch ones, but they reach 31 ft less far.
products.bestFor: People who want the thinnest fobs and several receivers for different items.
pros: Receivers are only about 0.2 inches thick
Stated 85 dB beep and a flashing LED on each fob
Six fobs cover keys, wallet, glasses and remotes
No app or phone needed, only a button press
cons: 100 ft range is 31 ft shorter than the 131 ft kits
Six coin cells must each be replaced around once a year
Radio only, so no location for keys left outside

products.name: Life360 Tile Bluetooth Tracker, iOS and Android
products.description:
The Life360 Tile is a Bluetooth fob that clips onto keys, a bag or a water bottle and works with both iPhone and Android. You ring the fob from the free app or track it on a map, and you can press the fob to ring your phone, even when silenced. It comes in 1, 2 and 4 pack sizes.

The listing also includes a discreet SOS alert for notifying loved ones and a link to the Life360 app for family maps. It does not state ring volume, water resistance, battery type or fob size, so we cannot compare it with the radio fobs on weight. The SOS and map extras only help if the family uses Life360.

The key advantage is that one fob works for a couple with different phones. A single fob on the main key ring is a sensible start. Unlike the Esky's six receivers, the Tile can show a location away from home, but it needs a phone where the Esky does not, and unlike the NVQ it does not state an IP67 rating.
products.bestFor: Couples or families who mix iPhone and Android and want one app for keys.
pros: One free app runs on both iPhone and Android
Press the fob to ring your phone, even on silent
Sold in 1, 2 and 4 packs for extra key sets
Optional Life360 link shows family and items on one map
cons: No ring volume, water rating or fob size appears in the listing
SOS and map extras need family members on Life360
Needs a phone and app, unlike the radio fobs

products.name: NVQ Key Finder, Works with Apple Find My
products.description:
The NVQ is a single Bluetooth fob that works through Apple's Find My app, so it suits iPhone owners. The listing states an IP67 water rating and a ring of up to 80 dB, and it describes the tag as a small IP67 luggage tracker. Lost Mode lets a finder see your contact details.

When keys are out of Bluetooth range, you check the last known spot on the map, relying on nearby Apple devices. The listing says clearly that it is not compatible with Android, and it is one fob per pack. A low battery alert tells you when to replace the cell, which avoids a quiet dead fob.

Of the six fobs here it is the one built for rain, jacket pockets and gym bags. Setup runs entirely through the Find My app. Compared with the Tile it states an IP67 rating that the Tile does not, and compared with the Esky it rings at up to 80 dB instead of 85 dB but works away from home.
products.bestFor: iPhone owners whose keys get rained on or carried in a gym bag.
pros: IP67 rating handles rain, splashes and brief dunks
Map shows the last known spot when keys leave home
Low battery alert warns you before the fob goes quiet
Lost Mode lets a finder see your contact details
cons: iPhone only, with no Android support at all
Rings at up to 80 dB, quieter than the 85 dB radio fobs
One fob per pack, so extra key sets cost more

products.name: Reyke Key Finder with Sound, RF Remote
products.description:
The Reyke is a four-fob radio kit with a handheld remote, large color-coded buttons and a stated 131 ft reach through walls, cushions and doors. Each fob beeps at 80 dB or louder and has a built-in LED flashlight. Four CR2032 batteries are included for the receivers.

The fobs come with a key chain attachment and are simple to clip on. The listing does not give weight or thickness, so we cannot rank them on bulk, and they are thicker than a slim Bluetooth tag. It cannot help once keys leave the house, so a set left at a restaurant stays lost.

Keep the remote on a hook near the door, and the system needs only occasional battery changes. Four fobs cover keys, a wallet, glasses and a spare set. At 131 ft it matches the Jegoteer and JTD, but its beep of 80 dB or louder is quieter than their 85 dB.
products.bestFor: Larger homes where a phone-free fob needs to cover several rooms.
pros: Claims a 131 ft reach through walls, cushions and doors
Large color-coded buttons are easy for any age
Fobs add an LED flashlight to the 80 dB or louder beep
Four CR2032 batteries are included in the box
cons: Listing gives no weight or thickness for the fobs
Beep of 80 dB or louder is quieter than the 85 dB kits
No map, so keys left outside the house are not findable

buyingCriteria.explanation: A fob rides on your keys every day, so bulk becomes an annoyance fast. The Esky receivers are about 0.2 inches thick, the Jegoteer's are 0.3 inches and about 5 g, and the Reyke, JTD, NVQ and Tile do not state dimensions. If your key ring already holds a car fob and several keys, favor the Esky or Jegoteer. Check the physical size before attaching more than one.

buyingCriteria.criterion: How the fob gets its signal
buyingCriteria.explanation: Radio fobs like the Jegoteer, JTD, Esky and Reyke beep when you press a button on a handheld remote and need no phone. Bluetooth fobs like the NVQ and Tile ring from an app and can report a last known location. A radio fob only works within about 100 to 131 ft of the remote. If your keys leave the house, a Bluetooth fob is the only type here that helps.

A small fob has a small speaker, so volume is worth checking. The Jegoteer and JTD state 85 dB, the Esky up to 85 dB, the Reyke 80 dB or louder, and the NVQ up to 80 dB. The Tile gives no figure. A fob buried in a coat will be muffled, so pick 85 dB if you often lose keys in pockets.

Keys get rained on, dropped and sat on. The NVQ is the only pick that states a water rating, IP67, which handles splashes and brief immersion. The Jegoteer, JTD, Esky, Reyke and Tile listings give no rating, so keep those in a pocket or bag. If your keys live outdoors, the NVQ is the safest published bet.

Radio fobs use coin cells that you must replace, and the Esky lists a CR2032 lasting up to a year per receiver. The Jegoteer lets you change a cell with a coin and its transmitter takes two AAA batteries. The NVQ sends a low battery alert. Pick a date each year to change every cell together.

buyingCriteria.criterion: What happens if the remote is lost
buyingCriteria.explanation: On a radio kit the fobs are useless without the remote, so it needs a fixed home such as a hook by the door. The Esky offers six fobs and the Jegoteer four, but each kit has one transmitter. Bluetooth fobs like the NVQ and Tile avoid the issue because the phone is the remote. Weigh that against owning a phone and an app.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fob size and weight
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared the stated dimensions and weight of each fob. The Esky lists 0.2 inches, the Jegoteer 1.9 x 1.2 x 0.3 inches and 5 g, and the other four give no size. A fob with a stated size earned more trust, because bulk on a key ring is a real daily cost.

howWeEvaluated.title: Signal and phone needs
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked how each fob finds your keys. The Jegoteer, JTD, Esky and Reyke use a radio remote with no phone, the NVQ needs an iPhone, and the Tile works on both phone types. Clear statements about compatibility counted heavily, since a fob you cannot pair is useless.

howWeEvaluated.title: Volume and range
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared stated beep levels and reach. The Jegoteer and JTD state 85 dB at 131 ft, the Reyke 80 dB or more at 131 ft, the Esky up to 85 dB at 100 ft, and the NVQ up to 80 dB. All figures are manufacturer claims, so we used them as relative guides.

howWeEvaluated.title: Durability and upkeep
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at water ratings and battery plans. The NVQ states IP67 with a low battery alert, the Esky lists a CR2032 per fob for up to a year, and the Reyke ships with four CR2032 cells. Where a listing was silent, as the Tile is on water and battery, we did not assume a spec.

howWeEvaluated.title: Lineup positioning
howWeEvaluated.description: We placed each pick by what it does best. The Jegoteer leads on weight and range, the JTD on a simple car key set, the Esky on thinness and receiver count, the Tile on mixed phones, the NVQ on IP67 and the Reyke on large buttons. We did not rank on popularity or review counts.

faq.q: What is a key finder fob?
faq.a: It is the small tag that attaches to your keys and either beeps when called or reports a location through a phone app. Radio fobs like the Jegoteer and Esky beep when you press a button on a handheld remote. Bluetooth fobs like the NVQ and Tile ring from an app.

The Esky states receivers about 0.2 inches thick, the thinnest figure in this lineup. The Jegoteer fobs are 0.3 inches and about 5 g. The Reyke, JTD, NVQ and Tile give no dimensions in their listings.

faq.q: Do I need a phone for a key finder fob?
faq.a: Not for the Jegoteer, JTD, Esky or Reyke, which use a radio remote. The NVQ needs an iPhone and the Find My app, and the Tile needs an iPhone or Android phone with the Tile app. Choose a radio kit if you want to avoid phones.

faq.q: Will a fob help if I lose my keys away from home?
faq.a: Radio fobs will not, because their range is about 100 to 131 ft. The NVQ and Tile can show a last known location through passing phones, but that depends on others being nearby. Neither is a real-time GPS tracker.

faq.q: How long do the fob batteries last?
faq.a: The Esky lists up to a year per CR2032 receiver, and the Reyke ships with four CR2032 cells. The NVQ sends a low battery alert. Pick one date each year to replace every cell, and test a fob by pressing its button now and then.

Mostly not. The NVQ is the only one that states a rating, IP67, which covers splashes and brief immersion. The Jegoteer, JTD, Esky, Reyke and Tile listings give no rating, so keep those out of rain and washing machines.
